body:
> Either way, there is no guarantee that the new agent and the agent that is running the worker share a process.

There is kind of an implication that shared workers will a separate process, and dedicated workers will use the same process. This is because the agent cluster boundary, which in the specification governs shared memory behavior, and thus in practice corresponds to process boundaries.

You can implement with something weaker than process boundaries, I think: IIUC, it's possible to be spec-conformant if the entire browser is single-process. But I think it's probably impossible to add process boundaries between a renderer process and a dedicated worker process, and still conform to the requirements of the ECMAScript spec's memory model for same-agent-cluster agents and realms.

> This implies that the `outside settings` variable is supposed to be the `fetchClient` EnvironmentSettingsObject for the fetch that will occur in the new Agent. However, the outside settings only exist in the owner Agent.

That's not really true. They exist in the spec, and can be accessed from anywhere in the spec. Despite "object" in the name, "environment settings objects"  are not JS objects. You can pass them anywhere.

> "environment settings objects" are not JS objects. You can pass them anywhere.

If this is the case, then we are probably modelling them incorrectly in LibWeb/Ladybird.

We have [`Environments`](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/webappapis.html#environment) as POD C++ objects, that hold a GC Pointer to a target browsing context.

[`Environment Settings Objects`](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/webappapis.html#environment-settings-object) on the other hand, are GC allocated objects (and is-a Environment) that retain strong ownership to GC allocated realm execution context, GC allocated module map, and two lists of GC allocated objects: the outstanding rejected promises weak set, and the about to be notified promises list.

We could probably serialize and pass an `Environment` around anywhere, but the ESO has a lot of extra baggage and algorithms that make that impossible (in our implementation). And the `run a worker` AO is specced to take an EnvironmentSettingsObject, not an Environment.

> But I think it's probably impossible to add process boundaries between a renderer process and a dedicated worker process, and still conform to the requirements of the ECMAScript spec's memory model for same-agent-cluster agents and realms.

Oh, that's unfortunate, because that's exactly what I'm prototyping this week :sweat_smile: . I thought that the only observable interactions between a DedicatedWorker and its owning Rendering process would be the message ports that they use to communicate? Though the spec steps that seem to want to be doing things in the Worker-owning Agent (renderer?) and the DedicatedWorker execution Agent did leave me scratching my head on how they'd end up working....

Looking at the ECMAScript spec for [Agent Clusters](https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-agent-clusters)

Note 1 says:
>   Programs within different [agents](https://tc39.es/ecma262/#agent) may share memory by unspecified means. At a minimum, the backing memory for SharedArrayBuffers can be shared among the [agents](https://tc39.es/ecma262/#agent) in the cluster.

Which sounds implementable to me as separate processes per agent, as long as the backing for SharedArrayBuffers uses some kind of IPC Shared Memory (such as POSIX SHM) that can fulfil the ordering requirements of the spec.

That is, as long as the "unspecified means" aren't relied on anywhere outside of SharedArrayBuffers :D

> thought that the only observable interactions between a DedicatedWorker and its owning Rendering process would be the message ports that they use to communicate?

The observable interactions I'm referring to are the impact on SharedArrayBuffer.

> some kind of IPC Shared Memory (such as POSIX SHM) that can fulfil the ordering requirements of the spec.

My understanding is that POSIX SHM cannot fulfill the ordering requirements, since the ordering requirements were derived from the common architecture that processors and OSes use for _thread_ boundaries, not process boundaries. But, I am only about 60% sure in this statement, as I am not an expert in this area. @syg is the person to ask.

Anyway, I'll close this issue, as I don't think there's any spec problem here. But happy to continue helping with architectural questions, either here or in Chat.
